UNIT 5

Unit V — SNMP, Intrusion Detection, Malware & Firewalls

SNMP architecture/community/SNMPv3, intruders, malware, IDS, trusted systems, firewall design and cases

1 · Terminology2 · Short Q&A3 · 10-mark answers4 · Comparisons & recall

1. Terminology — learn these first

SNMP

Simple Network Management Protocol used to monitor/control managed network devices.

Manager / management station

System that runs the management application and queries or configures agents.

Agent

Software on a managed device that exposes management information and responds to requests.

MIB

Management Information Base: conceptual collection/tree of managed objects.

OID

Object Identifier that names an object in the management information tree.

Get / GetNext / GetBulk

Operations to read an object, navigate to the next object or retrieve multiple values efficiently.

Set

Manager request to change a managed object.

Trap / Inform

Notifications from an agent; an Inform typically requests acknowledgment.

SNMP community

Shared text-like value used as a simple community-based access/authentication mechanism in SNMPv1/v2c.

SNMPv3 USM

User-based Security Model providing message integrity, authentication and optional privacy.

VACM

View-Based Access Control Model defining which management objects a user may access.

Intruder

Person who gains access or privileges without authorization or abuses legitimate privileges.

Masquerader / misfeasor / clandestine user

Outsider using another account / legitimate user misusing rights / user who seizes supervisory control to evade auditing.

Malware

Software intended to damage, disrupt, spy on or gain unauthorized control.

Virus / worm

Virus attaches to a host program; worm propagates across systems, typically without a host program.

Trojan horse / backdoor

Software with hidden harmful functionality / secret path that bypasses normal access controls.

IDS

Intrusion Detection System that analyzes activity and raises alerts for suspicious behavior.

False positive / false negative

Legitimate activity flagged as attack / actual attack missed.

Firewall

Enforcement point controlling traffic between networks according to policy.

Packet filter / stateful firewall / proxy

Filters packet fields / tracks connection state / intermediates at application or circuit level.

Bastion host

Hardened system exposed to a less-trusted network and designed to withstand attack.

Trusted system

System whose hardware/software and controls can enforce a defined security policy.

Secure multiparty computation

Protocol allowing parties to compute a function over private inputs while limiting what each learns.

XSS

Cross-site scripting: untrusted content is executed as script in another user’s browser under a vulnerable site’s origin.

2. Short-answer question bank

Attempt each answer in 2–4 lines. The section contains more than 20 questions where useful to cover the unit's syllabus points.

01. What is SNMP used for?
Answer: Monitoring and management of routers, switches, servers, printers and other network devices.
02. Name the four SNMP model elements.
Answer: Management station, management agent, management information base (MIB) and management protocol.
03. What is the MIB?
Answer: A conceptual collection/tree of managed objects that an agent exposes for reading or writing.
04. What does SNMP Get do?
Answer: Reads the value of a named managed object.
05. What does SNMP Set do?
Answer: Requests a managed object value to be changed.
06. What is an SNMP Trap?
Answer: An asynchronous notification sent by an agent without waiting for a manager request.
07. What is an SNMP community?
Answer: A shared value used by SNMPv1/v2c to associate requests with access privileges.
08. Why is SNMPv1 community security weak?
Answer: Community strings are not strong modern cryptographic authentication and SNMPv1 lacks privacy protection.
09. Name two SNMPv3 security components.
Answer: USM for message security and VACM for access control.
10. What is a masquerader?
Answer: An unauthorized outsider who obtains access using another user’s identity or account.
11. What is a misfeasor?
Answer: A legitimate user who accesses unauthorized resources or abuses their privileges.
12. What is a clandestine user?
Answer: An attacker who gains supervisory control to evade access controls or audit collection.
13. Differentiate virus and worm.
Answer: A virus attaches to a host program; a worm self-propagates between computers over networks.
14. What is a logic bomb?
Answer: Code that triggers a harmful action when a particular condition/event occurs.
15. What is a Trojan horse?
Answer: A seemingly useful program containing hidden unwanted or harmful functionality.
16. What are the four common virus phases?
Answer: Dormant, propagation, triggering and execution.
17. What is an IDS?
Answer: A system that analyzes activity/events to detect suspicious or unauthorized behavior.
18. Define false positive and false negative.
Answer: False positive flags legitimate behavior; false negative fails to identify a real attack.
19. State three firewall design goals.
Answer: All relevant traffic passes through it; only policy-authorized traffic is allowed; the firewall itself is hardened.
20. Name common firewall types.
Answer: Packet-filtering, stateful inspection, application-level gateway/proxy and circuit-level gateway.
21. What is a trusted system?
Answer: A system designed and evaluated to enforce a stated security policy using controlled mechanisms.
22. What is single sign-on (SSO)?
Answer: One authenticated login/session grants access to multiple related services without repeated logins.
23. What is cross-site scripting?
Answer: An injection flaw where untrusted input becomes executable script in a victim’s browser.
24. What is secure multiparty computation?
Answer: A way for parties to compute a joint result without revealing their private inputs beyond allowed output.

3. Important 10-mark answers

Model answers use headings and a logical sequence so you can reproduce them in the exam. Diagrams from the source PDFs are embedded where helpful.

10 MARKS Explain SNMP architecture, components and principal operations.

Purpose. SNMP manages network equipment by exposing management data and offering remote read/configuration operations. Its classic architecture includes a management station, agents running on managed devices, a MIB and the SNMP protocol carried over the network.

Components. The management station provides the operator interface and management applications. An agent obtains local device data and responds to manager requests. The MIB models resources as objects with names/identifiers and values; OIDs identify objects in a hierarchical tree. The protocol defines request and response messages and notifications.

Core operations. Get retrieves values; GetNext walks the MIB tree; GetBulk retrieves groups efficiently in later versions; Set changes a value; Response acknowledges/returns results; Trap sends an asynchronous notification; Inform sends a notification for which acknowledgment is expected in versions that support it.

Flow. A manager sends a request to an agent. The agent checks access, queries the relevant managed object and sends a response. When a significant event occurs, the agent can send a notification to the configured manager.

Conclusion. Memorize manager → agent → MIB object; Get reads, Set writes, Trap notifies.

10 MARKS Compare SNMPv1 community facility with SNMPv3 security architecture.

SNMPv1 community model. A community associates managers and agents with a named community and access profile. A community name is included in protocol messages and is used as a simple shared value. The agent can limit what managers can read/write through MIB views and access policy. The notes list Get, Set and Notify as important capabilities.

Limitations. Community strings are not a substitute for modern cryptographic authentication, can be exposed on the network, and SNMPv1 lacks strong confidentiality. Read-write community exposure is particularly risky; devices should not be exposed to untrusted networks.

SNMPv3 architecture. SNMP entities contain an SNMP engine plus applications. Message-processing models support different protocol versions; the security subsystem applies security processing; access control decides which managed objects can be accessed. Traditional application roles include command generator, command responder, notification originator/receiver and proxy forwarder.

USM and VACM. The User-based Security Model provides authentication and integrity, and optional privacy/encryption. The View-Based Access Control Model maps users/groups and contexts to permitted MIB views and read/write/notify access.

FeatureSNMPv1 community facilitySNMPv3
Identity/securityShared community valueUser-based security with configured credentials/keys
Integrity/authenticationWeak by modern standardsUSM supports message authentication and integrity
ConfidentialityNo strong message privacyOptional privacy protection
Access controlCommunity-associated MIB views/profilesVACM views and access policies
Recommended directionLegacy/limited trusted networks onlyPrefer modern secured configuration

Conclusion. SNMPv1 is simple but weak; SNMPv3 adds proper message security and granular access control. Secure deployments restrict management traffic, use least privilege and protect credentials.

10 MARKS Explain intruder categories, password attacks and countermeasures.

Intruder types. (1) Masquerader: outsider who uses another user's account. (2) Misfeasor: legitimate user who accesses unauthorized data or abuses privileges. (3) Clandestine user: gains supervisory control and evades auditing/access controls. The first is likely an outsider, the second usually an insider, and the third can be either.

Password attacks. Common techniques include trying default passwords, exhaustive guessing of short passwords, dictionary/common-password guesses, using personal information, credential theft through Trojan software and tapping insecure remote logins. Poorly protected password files create additional risk.

Password protection in the notes. Store a one-way transformation rather than plaintext, and restrict access to password-verification data. Modern best practice uses a unique salt and a deliberately slow password-hashing function rather than a fast general-purpose hash. Apply rate limiting, MFA, breached-password screening and monitoring; never store reversible plaintext passwords.

Countermeasures. Remove default accounts/credentials, require long unique passwords, use a password manager and MFA, enforce least privilege, harden systems, patch vulnerabilities, monitor logs, protect administrative access, segment systems and investigate suspicious activity. Prevention is important, but detection and incident response are also necessary because controls may fail.

Conclusion. Write the three categories exactly, then list password-attack methods and layered preventive/detective controls.

10 MARKS Explain viruses and related threats, the virus life cycle and countermeasures.

Malicious-program examples. A virus attaches to a host program and spreads when that program runs; a worm is an independent program that propagates over networks; a logic bomb triggers under a condition; a Trojan horse hides extra functionality in an apparently useful program; a backdoor bypasses normal controls; keyloggers capture keystrokes; rootkits conceal privileged compromise; zombies are infected machines used to launch attacks.

Four virus phases. (1) Dormant: inactive while awaiting a trigger (not every virus has this stage). (2) Propagation: copies itself into other files or system areas. (3) Triggering: condition activates its intended behavior. (4) Execution: payload runs, harmless or damaging.

Other types in the notes. Parasitic viruses attach to executable files; memory-resident viruses stay in main memory; boot-sector viruses infect boot records; stealth viruses hide from detection; polymorphic viruses change appearance; metamorphic viruses rewrite themselves; macro viruses use document-embedded macros.

Countermeasures. Keep operating systems and applications updated; use reputable endpoint protection; enable least privilege and application controls; block suspicious macros and attachments; filter email/web downloads; segment backups; maintain offline/immutable backups; restrict removable media; monitor unusual behavior; isolate infected systems and follow incident-response procedures.

Conclusion. Explain host dependency (virus) versus network propagation (worm), memorize D-P-T-E, and connect controls to prevention, detection, containment and recovery.

10 MARKS Explain intrusion detection systems, approaches and detection errors.

IDS purpose. Intrusion detection is a second line of defense when prevention fails. It identifies suspicious events, alerts administrators, may support containment and provides data about attacker techniques to improve defenses.

Detection approaches. Signature/misuse-based detection compares events with known attack patterns; it is often clear for known attacks but may miss new variations. Anomaly-based detection compares activity with a baseline or learned model of normal behavior; it can detect novel behavior but may trigger more false alarms. Host-based IDS observes activity on a host; network-based IDS analyzes traffic at a network vantage point. Hybrid deployments combine sources.

Errors. A false positive flags legitimate activity as malicious. A false negative fails to detect an actual intrusion. A very sensitive or “loose” detection threshold tends to catch more suspicious events but may raise more false positives; a strict threshold may reduce false positives but miss attacks.

Operational cycle. Collect events → normalize/enrich → detect and correlate → alert/triage → contain/investigate → record lessons and tune rules. Useful signals include failed logins, unusual privilege use, unexpected network flows, changes to critical files and anomalous process behavior.

Conclusion. No detector is perfect. Combine IDS with prevention, logging, threat hunting, endpoint controls and a response plan.

10 MARKS Explain firewall design principles, types and configurations.

Definition. A firewall enforces a security policy between networks of different trust levels. It creates a controlled choke point, restricts potentially dangerous services and can log traffic for audit. It can also serve as a VPN/IPSec platform and sometimes perform NAT.

Three core design goals. (1) All relevant traffic between inside and outside must pass through the firewall. (2) Only traffic authorized by the local security policy is allowed. (3) The firewall itself must be resistant to penetration and securely administered.

Control techniques. Service control decides which network services are allowed; direction control determines allowed traffic directions; user control applies user-specific restrictions; behavior control limits how services may be used.

Types. Packet-filter firewall evaluates header fields such as IP addresses, ports and protocol. Stateful inspection tracks connection state. Application-level gateway/proxy terminates and intermediates application traffic, enabling deeper inspection but increasing cost/latency. Circuit-level gateway controls session establishment and circuit behavior without full application-content inspection.

Configurations. A screened-host architecture exposes a hardened bastion host; a dual-homed bastion uses separate interfaces; a screened-subnet/DMZ creates an intermediate network for public-facing services. Multiple layers help prevent a single compromise from exposing the internal LAN.

Limitations. Firewalls do not automatically protect against insider misuse, traffic that bypasses the firewall, malware in allowed traffic, or vulnerabilities in permitted applications. Endpoint security, patching, monitoring and secure application design remain necessary.

Conclusion. State the three goals, classify the firewall types and draw a perimeter/DMZ/internal-network configuration with the bastion host labeled.

10 MARKS Explain trusted systems and security-policy enforcement.

Trusted system. A trusted system is designed so that its hardware/software mechanisms can enforce a defined security policy. “Trusted” does not mean invulnerable; it means the system’s security-relevant behavior is controlled, testable and relied upon within a stated assurance boundary.

Important concepts. Identification and authentication establish a subject identity; authorization and access-control mechanisms determine allowed actions; security labels/classifications can constrain information flow; audit mechanisms record security-relevant events; a protected reference monitor mediates access to objects. The reference-monitor idea requires complete mediation, tamper resistance and a design small enough to analyze (the classic exam formulation).

Operational principles. Least privilege, separation of duties, secure defaults, defense in depth, trusted boot, access reviews, logging, patching and change control support policy enforcement. A secure operating system and hardened bastion hosts can be part of a trusted-system design.

Conclusion. Define the policy first, explain controlled access and auditing, then describe why trust rests on verifiable mechanisms and assurance—not on a claim that the system cannot fail.

10 MARKS Discuss the syllabus case studies: secure multiparty computation, virtual elections, SSO, inter-branch payments and XSS.

1. Secure multiparty computation (MPC). Several parties compute a joint function over private inputs without revealing their raw inputs beyond what the output necessarily reveals. Example: several banks determine a risk total without sharing each customer's complete data. Key concerns are input privacy, correctness, collusion assumptions, malicious participants and communication cost.

2. Virtual elections. A secure electronic election must authenticate eligible voters, prevent duplicate votes, preserve ballot secrecy, maintain ballot integrity, count correctly and provide auditability. Challenges include coercion resistance, endpoint compromise, voter-verifiability, ballot secrecy and avoiding a trusted counting point that can silently alter results.

3. Single sign-on (SSO). A user authenticates once to an identity provider and obtains a token/assertion for authorized relying applications. Benefits are less password reuse and consistent access control; risks include a high-value identity provider, token theft, misconfigured trust and overly broad sessions. Use MFA, short token lifetimes, audience/issuer validation, secure redirects and least privilege.

4. Secure inter-branch payment transaction. Authenticate branch systems, establish protected channel keys, authorize the transaction, protect amount/account/sequence data with integrity checks, prevent replay with unique transaction IDs/nonces, sign or MAC the transaction, log both sides and reconcile acknowledgments. Retries should be idempotent so duplicate messages do not double-charge.

5. Cross-site scripting (XSS). Untrusted input is interpreted as script in a victim’s browser under a trusted site’s origin. Types include stored, reflected and DOM-based. Impact can include session theft, forged UI/actions and data exposure. Defenses: context-aware output encoding, safe templating, sanitization where rich HTML is allowed, avoid unsafe DOM sinks, Content Security Policy as defense in depth, HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookies and security testing.

Conclusion. For every case, name the protected property, threat, control and residual risk. These case-study topics are explicitly present in the syllabus but receive limited dedicated detail in the supplied notes, so this section provides a concise syllabus-aligned exam framework.

High-yield comparisons

PairDifference
Virus vs wormVirus attaches to a host program; worm independently propagates between systems.
Trojan vs backdoorTrojan disguises hidden behavior as useful software; backdoor is a secret access path.
Signature IDS vs anomaly IDSKnown patterns vs deviations from normal behavior.
False positive vs false negativeBenign activity flagged vs malicious activity missed.
Packet filter vs application proxyHeader-based filtering vs application-aware intermediation.
SNMPv1 vs SNMPv3Community-based legacy model vs USM message security plus VACM access control.

Last-minute recall

SNMP: Manager, Agent, MIB, Protocol. Get reads; Set writes; Trap alerts.
Intruders: Masquerader, Misfeasor, Clandestine user.
Virus phases: D-P-T-E = Dormant, Propagation, Triggering, Execution.
Firewall: all traffic passes, policy permits only allowed traffic, firewall is hardened.
IDS: tune the tradeoff between false positives and false negatives.

Must-practice diagrams

Draw from memory: (1) network-security model, (2) Feistel/DES or AES rounds, (3) RSA/Diffie–Hellman key flow, (4) MAC/HMAC, (5) Kerberos ticket flow, (6) X.509 certificate chain, (7) IPSec transport vs tunnel + AH/ESP, (8) TLS handshake, (9) SNMP manager-agent-MIB, (10) firewall/DMZ.

When writing a 10-mark answer

  1. Start with a precise definition and state the security problem being solved.
  2. Draw a labeled architecture or flow where applicable.
  3. Explain each block/step in order, using formulas for algorithms.
  4. Include two benefits and one limitation or security caveat.
  5. Finish with a 2-line summary and one example/application.
